$$

$$

Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and

$$\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=0-(-1)=1.$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D)&=\iint_D\text{d}A\\&=\iint_D(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y})\,\text{d}A\\&=\oint_C P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}$$

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$\oint_C P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y=-\oint_C y\,\text{d}x.$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$r'(t)=\langle -7\sin t,3\cos t\rangle.$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$\begin{aligned}-\oint_C y\,\text{d}x&=-\int_0^{2\pi}3\sin t\cdot(-7\sin t)\,\text{d}t\\&=21\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2 t\,\text{d}t\\&=21\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{1-\cos 2t}{2}\,\text{d}t\\&=\int_0^{2\pi}\left(\frac{21}{2}-\frac{21}{2}\cos 2t\right)\,\text{d}t\\&=\left[\frac{21}{2}t-\frac{21}{4}\sin 2t\right]_0^{2\pi}\\&=\left(21 \pi-0\right)-\left(0-0\right)\\&=21 \pi\end{aligned}$$

Therefore, we conclude that $\text{Area}(D)=21 \pi.$

Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/fa/fa98f3db31860a463d0a551d5297895e61a6c041d852c04de04c44a194510961.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=y\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y{x}^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=\sqrt[3]{x}+y.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3{x}^{2}y+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(3{x}^{2}y+1)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{3}y+x)\,{|}_{-1}^{1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[((1)^{3}y+1)-((-1)^{3}y+(-1))]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(2y+2)\,dy \\  & =[{y}^{2}+2y]_{0}^{2} \\  & =((2)^{2}+2(2))-0 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Let $f(x)=\sqrt{x-3}.$ We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=x-3.$ Then $f=\sqrt{u}={u}^{1/2}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2}{u}^{-1/2}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1.

$$

question.:question/problem:

$$

$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iiint_R f(x,y,z)\,dV=\iiint_\Delta f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta.
$$

If $(r,\theta,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x=r\cos\theta,\quad y=r\sin\theta,\quad z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](images/05/0505715b5e78700e63d98fc2c1db8e7d4a3074b3e06f4202de1ce5a6831f7571.png)

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $2$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=0=0,$ and

- bounded above by $z=1=1.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

$$
\Delta=\{(r,\theta,z):0\le r\le 2,\ 0\le\theta<2\cdot \pi,\ 0\le z\le 1\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\iiint_R 4\cdot \sqrt{(x)^{2}+(y)^{2}}\,dV &=\iiint_\Delta (4\cdot \sqrt{(r\cdot \cos(\theta))^2+(r\cdot \sin(\theta))^2})\cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta \\ &=\int_{0}^{2\cdot \pi}\int_0^{2}\int_{0}^{1}4\cdot (r)^{2}\,dz\,dr\,d\theta \\ &=\int_{0}^{2\cdot \pi}\int_0^{2}4\cdot (r)^{2}[z]_{z=0}^{z=1}\,dr\,d\theta \\ &=\int_{0}^{2\cdot \pi}\int_0^{2}4\cdot (r)^{2}((1)-(0))\,dr\,d\theta \\ &=\int_{0}^{2\cdot \pi}\int_0^{2}4\cdot (r)^{2}\,dr\,d\theta \\ &=\int_{0}^{2\cdot \pi}[\frac{4}{3}\cdot (r)^{3}]_{r=0}^{r=2}\,d\theta \\ &=\int_{0}^{2\cdot \pi}(\frac{4}{3}\cdot ((2))^{3})-(\frac{4}{3}\cdot ((0))^{3})\,d\theta \\ &=\int_{0}^{2\cdot \pi}\left(\frac{32}{3}\right)-(0)\,d\theta \\ &=\int_{0}^{2\cdot \pi}\frac{32}{3}\,d\theta \\ &=[\frac{32}{3}\cdot \theta]_{\theta=0}^{\theta=2\cdot \pi} \\ &=(\frac{64}{3}\cdot \pi)-(0) \\ &=\frac{64}{3}\cdot \pi\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=x$ along the line $y=2 x,$ $\,0\le x\le 3.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)=2 t.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle t,2 t\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le 3
$$

Computing $\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)$ and $\|\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)&=\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\mathbf i+\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}\mathbf j \\ &=\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}(t)\mathbf i+\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}(2 t)\mathbf j \\ &=\mathbf i+(2)\mathbf j \\ \|\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)\|&=\sqrt{\left(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}\right)^2} \\ &=\sqrt{1^2+(2)^2} \\ &=\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t))&=t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm ds&=\int_{0}^{3}f(r(t))\|\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)\|\,\mathrm dt \\ &=\int_{0}^{3}(t)(\sqrt{5})\,\mathrm dt \\ &=\left[\frac{\sqrt{5} t^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{3} \\ &=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\left((3)^{2}-(0)^{2}\right) \\ &=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\left(9-0\right) \\ &=\frac{9 \sqrt{5}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t+2)j \\  & =i+3\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{10}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={t}^{2}+(3t+2)={t}^{2}+3t+2.\end{aligned}

$$

question.:question/problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=2{y}^{2}$ along the curve $y={e}^{x},$ $\,0\le x\le \ln{\left(4 \right)}.$

Notice that the given curve is of the form $y=y(x).$ Therefore, by setting $x=t,$ we have $y=y(t)={e}^{t}.$ This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨t,\,{e}^{t}⟩,\,0\le t\le \ln{\left(4 \right)}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})j \\  & =i+{e}^{t}j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{({e}^{t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{e}^{2t}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=2{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2({e}^{t})^{2}=2{e}^{2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\ln{\left(4 \right)}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\ln{\left(4 \right)}}2{e}^{2t}\cdot \sqrt{1+{e}^{2t}}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\ln{\left(4 \right)}}2{e}^{2t}\,\sqrt{1+{e}^{2t}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=1+{e}^{2t}$, $\text{d}u=2{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t$ as follows:  

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\ln{\left(4 \right)}}2{e}^{2t}\,\sqrt{1+{e}^{2t}}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{2}^{17}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}{|}_{2}^{17} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}({17}^{3/2}-{2}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(17 \sqrt{17}-2\sqrt{2}) \\  & =- \frac{4 \sqrt{2}}{3} + \frac{34 \sqrt{17}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$
